claims.text: Adding 0.5 wt% yttrium to a WMoTaNbV-based refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The yttrium addition will segregate to the oxide/alloy interface during oxidation.
Yttrium segregation will improve the adherence of the protective oxide scale.
Yttrium segregation will improve the continuity of the protective oxide scale.
At high temperature, added yttrium migrates from the alloy matrix to the oxide/alloy interface.
Interfacial yttrium reduces the energy of the oxide/alloy interface.
Reduced oxide/alloy interfacial energy enhances oxide-scale adhesion.
The protective oxide on the yttrium-modified WMoTaNbV alloy is likely to be alumina or a mixture of oxides.
A more adherent and continuous oxide scale will limit oxygen ingress.
Limiting oxygen ingress will slow oxidation kinetics.
At 1100°C in laboratory air for 100 hours, the yttrium-doped alloy will have a lower oxidation rate than the undoped alloy.
At 1100°C in laboratory air for 100 hours, the yttrium-doped alloy will exhibit lower weight gain than the undoped alloy.
At 1100°C in laboratory air for 100 hours, the yttrium-doped alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than the undoped alloy.
Untreated WMoTaNbV typically has relatively high oxidation rates under the stated exposure conditions.
Untreated WMoTaNbV typically forms a less coherent oxide scale under the stated exposure conditions.

contradictions.description: The stated alloy contains W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V, and added Y but no aluminum, whereas the mechanism identifies alumina as a likely protective oxide. Alumina formation is inconsistent with the stated composition unless an unmentioned aluminum source is present.
